title: Speech
hook: precept four: refrain from false speech

segments.voice: Yesterday, precept three, sexual conduct: harm, not shame, is the measure. Your line was no harm in love.

I'm five minutes away, said from the couch. I love it, said about the sweater. Sorry, just saw this, about a text that arrived three hours ago. Small untrue things, the kind that grease the day. Nobody gets hurt, goes the thinking. The fourth precept is about exactly these words, and the Pali Canon teaches it with a vivid scene: a father, a small boy, and a dipper of water.
screen: `I'M FIVE MINUTES AWAY.` → `I LOVE THE SWEATER.` → `A FATHER, A BOY, A DIPPER.`

segments.voice: In Pali: Musavada veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from false speech. Musa means false; vada, speech. Now the story. The Buddha's son, Rahula, had joined the order as a boy. One evening the Buddha visited him, and Rahula set out water for his feet. The Buddha washed, left a little water in the dipper, and asked: do you see this small amount? That's how little of the spiritual life is in someone who isn't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie. He tossed the water out: that's how easily it's thrown away. He turned the dipper upside down: that's how it's overturned. He turned it back, empty: that's how empty it is. Then something gentle and practical: don't tell a lie, even as a joke. Before you act or speak, look, the way you'd look in a mirror, and ask whether it will harm anyone. Another discourse adds the other half. Asked whether he ever said unwelcome things, the Buddha pointed to a baby on a prince's lap. If the child had a stick or a stone in its mouth, you'd take it out, even if it drew a little blood, out of compassion. He speaks what is true and helpful, he said, and he knows the right time to say it. So the precept isn't permission to be brutal. It's truth, with care about timing and kindness. The small lie trades a moment of comfort for a little less trust. The precept trains the other trade.
screen: `MUSA: FALSE. VADA: SPEECH.` · `THE DIPPER: A LITTLE WATER LEFT.` · `LOOK IN THE MIRROR FIRST.` · `TRUE, HELPFUL, AT THE RIGHT TIME.` · then, large: `SAY WHAT'S TRUE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day and find one small untrue thing you said; no big confession, just notice what it was protecting: your comfort, their feelings, your image. Then picture that moment and imagine the true version, said kindly. Hear how it sounds; maybe it's easier than you thought.
Speech. The fourth precept: a training to refrain from false speech, and to say what's true and helpful, at the right time.
Your line: say what's true. True, helpful, and at the right time. That's day one hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhists recite the fourth precept, to refrain from false speech, with the other four, and many teachers pair it with the fuller idea of right speech: true, helpful, kind and well timed.

fork.setup: a baby on your lap has put a sharp stone in its mouth. taking it out will make the baby cry. what do you do?
options: take it out, gently, even if it hurts.
fork.reveal: the Buddha used this picture for hard truths: you take it out, out of compassion, and you choose the right moment.

original.note: Pali: false speech (musa, false + vada, speech); the fourth precept is to refrain from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't tell big lies.
what it means: a training in truth, even in small things, spoken kindly and at the right time.
what a scholar hears: MN 61 has the dipper and the mirror for Rahula; MN 58 adds the criteria of true, beneficial and timely speech.
recall: a collected, steady mind that can stay put
the first part of a step: the heel rising

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 61 (Ambalatthika Rahulovada Sutta), the dipper and the mirror

The baby and the stick or pebble, and true / beneficial / timely speech, are paraphrased from MN 58.
